title: cubic blog: Which AI Code Reviewer Auto-Generates a Summary of What a Pull Request Actually Changes?
summary: Set up AI pull request review on GitHub with cubic. Configure review rules, reduce noisy comments, and measure useful fixes without skipping human review.
body_markdown:
AI pull request review checks a code change before it merges and posts findings on the pull request. A useful AI reviewer reads the diff with relevant repository context, explains a concrete failure, and points to the code that needs attention. It can give a human reviewer an earlier first pass on bugs, security issues and team conventions.


To set up AI code review on GitHub, connect a reviewer to one repository, open a PR, add your team's review rules, and check whether its comments lead to useful fixes. Keep tests and your existing approval requirements in place while you evaluate it.


We build cubic. The walkthrough below uses cubic; the evaluation checklist applies to any AI pull request reviewer. Our[AI code review guide](https://www.cubic.dev/ai-code-review) explains the broader category.


## What should an AI pull request reviewer catch?


Look for findings tied to behavior, with enough evidence for someone to check them. "This could be cleaner" is less useful than an explanation of which request fails, why it fails and where the fix belongs.


Use examples like these when evaluating a reviewer on your own code. They illustrate the kinds of problems to test for, rather than a promise that a tool will catch every one.


Change


Useful review question


What to verify


An endpoint accepts a record ID


Can one account read or modify another account's record?


Trace authorization through the handler, service and query.


A webhook retries failed requests


Can the same event charge a customer twice?


Check idempotency and the transaction boundary.


An API response changes shape


Do existing callers still handle the response?


Read the caller and its error handling alongside the changed endpoint.


A background job changes


Does a partial failure leave work permanently stuck?


Check retries, cleanup and the recovery path.


Keep formatters, type checks, tests and static analysis in CI. AI review can miss a real issue or invent one. A clean review does not establish that the code is correct, and an accepted suggestion does not establish that every part of the suggestion was necessary.

## How to set up AI pull request review on GitHub


Use one active repository for the pilot. Pick a team willing to explain wrong findings and enough ordinary PRs to see how the reviewer behaves beyond a demonstration.


### 1. Connect the cubic GitHub App


[Sign up for cubic](https://www.cubic.dev/sign-up) with GitHub and choose the organization that owns the repository. Select **Only select repositories** for the pilot and review the requested permissions. If you cannot install the app yourself, your organization's policy may require an owner to approve the request;[GitHub's installation guide](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/using-github-apps/installing-a-github-app-from-a-third-party) explains those permissions and roles.


The[cubic quickstart](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/quickstart) walks through the connection and first review. The trial lasts seven days and requires no credit card.


### 2. Trigger the first review


Open a new pull request in the connected repository. cubic starts reviewing new PRs automatically. To review an existing PR, post:


```text
@ cubic  - dev  - ai   review   this    PR
```


```text
@ cubic  - dev  - ai   review   this    PR
```


```text
@ cubic  - dev  - ai   review   this    PR
```


Read the inline findings and check the explanation against the actual code path. Confirm the failure before applying a suggested fix. Draft PRs are skipped unless draft review is enabled in your repository's[AI review settings](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/ai-review-settings) .


### 3. Give the reviewer a specific team rule


Tell the reviewer what your team wants it to flag. Broad instructions such as "follow best practices" leave too much room for interpretation. A useful rule names the code it applies to, the failure to prevent and the preferred pattern.


For example, a multi-tenant application might use this rule:


> In API handlers that load tenant-owned records, flag queries that use only the record ID without checking the authenticated tenant. Use the shared tenant-scoped query helper. Public catalog endpoints are exempt.


In cubic, create that check as a[custom agent](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/custom-agents) and limit it to the relevant paths. Use the[agents library](https://www.cubic.dev/agents) for other starting points. Turn repeated review comments from your senior engineers into explicit rules; our[code review standards](https://www.cubic.dev/standards) page covers how to define them.


### 4. Version review settings with the repository


Once the pilot settings are useful, commit a[cubic.yaml configuration](https://docs.cubic.dev/configure/cubic-yaml) at the repository root. This example keeps incremental reviews on, skips drafts and generated output, and leaves auto-approval disabled:


```text
version :    1
reviews :
enabled :    true
sensitivity :    medium
incremental_commits :    true
check_drafts :    false
resolve_threads_when_addressed :    true
auto_approve_behavior :    disabled
auto_approve :    disabled
ignore :
files :
-  'dist/**'
-  'generated/**'
pr_labels :
-  'skip-review'
```

cubic reads this configuration from the default branch, so merge it before checking its effect on later reviews. Repository settings override organization defaults field by field. If you need shared defaults across repositories, use a` cubic-config` repository.


### 5. Respond to findings and check the next push


Fix a valid issue, explain a false positive, or record why the finding is out of scope. Make the reason concrete. "This route is intentionally public; authentication is required only for writes" is useful feedback.


cubic can turn feedback that states a reusable rule into a team learning. One-off requests and replies such as "thanks" do not become rules. Review the resulting guidance under **AI review → Learnings** ; the[memory and learning documentation](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/memory-and-learning) explains how to edit it.


If your team uses **Fix with cubic** , inspect the resulting change and run the relevant checks before merging. An AI-generated fix needs review too.


## Make the human review easier in cubic


Finding bugs is one part of review. A person still needs to understand what the PR changes and whether that behavior is right.


Open the same PR in cubic by replacing` github.com` with` cubic.dev` in its URL, or find it in your[pull request inbox](https://docs.cubic.dev/code-review-platform/dashboard) . The[cubic review page](https://docs.cubic.dev/code-review-platform/overview) groups related files, explains each group and places the core change first.


-


**Follow the change across files.** Read an endpoint, its caller and its tests together.


-


**Ask for a walkthrough.** Enter` tour this PR` in AI chat, then ask questions about the code that needs your judgment.


-


**Review the next push.** Use **Since your last review** to focus on changes made after your earlier pass.


-


**Submit the review.** Comments, approvals and requests for changes sync back to GitHub.


Keep large work in reviewable pieces. If one change depends on another, our[stacked pull requests guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/stacked-pull-requests) explains how to split the work while keeping the branch dependencies clear.


## Keep AI PR review useful instead of noisy


Treat configuration as part of the pilot. When engineers dismiss a finding, find out whether the problem was missing context, a bad rule or an incorrect conclusion.


-


**Leave drafts out of the first rollout.** Review work when the author is ready for feedback.


-


**Exclude generated output deliberately.** Keep source files and the generator under review. Avoid blanket exclusions for tests, migrations or security-sensitive files.


-


**Keep incremental reviews enabled.** cubic checks new commits and posts new issues rather than repeating earlier findings. Auto-resolve can close threads when it detects a fix; inspect important fixes yourself.


-


**Tighten rules that produce weak findings.** Add a path, an exception or a concrete failure condition before adding more rules.


-


**Evaluate one reviewer at a time.** This makes it easier to attribute useful findings and avoid duplicate comments during the pilot.


For a migration, authorization change or payment flow, request a deeper pass with` @cubic-dev-ai ultrareview` .[Ultrareview](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/ultrareview) performs multi-pass analysis and is available on paid and trial plans. It uses the reviewed-lines allowance at three times the standard rate, so include that in the pilot's usage budget.


## Measure useful fixes, missed issues and review time


Set a baseline before installation and keep the pilot's repository, period and PR mix visible. Count comments only as a workload measure. The outcomes matter more.


Measure


How to assess it


Confirmed useful findings


Sample comments and check whether they identify a real problem. Separate necessary fixes from optional suggestions.


Fix rate


Track how many posted issues a later commit addresses. Audit a sample of the detected fixes.


Missed issues


Record bugs humans, tests or incidents found that the reviewer missed. Include their severity.


Review effort and merge time


Compare similar-sized PRs and note changes in team load, weekends and release activity.


Cost per merged PR


Use the pilot's actual charges and include review usage and reruns.


In cubic's[AI review analytics](https://docs.cubic.dev/analytics/ai-review) , **Issues fixed** tracks findings that a later commit appears to resolve. That automated check can be wrong: open the issue and inspect its fix commit to confirm. **Time to merge** is a median from PR opening to merge, including drafts and weekends. A faster median alone does not prove that AI review caused the improvement.


A fix rate is an adoption signal, not a complete accuracy score. It does not tell you how many real bugs were missed. Use the sampling above alongside our[pull request metrics guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/code-review-metrics) to decide whether to expand the rollout.


## Keep approval policy separate from review comments


Start with AI comments and your existing human approvals. Keep CI, required reviewers and code-owner requirements configured through[GitHub branch protection](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches) or your organization's rulesets.


If you later want automatic approval for narrowly defined changes, test cubic's[auto-approval](https://docs.cubic.dev/ai-review/auto-approval) in **Shadow** mode first. It shows which PRs would be approved without submitting real approvals. Choose **Low-risk only** or a specific custom policy, exclude sensitive paths, and compare the results with your reviewers' decisions before enabling **Live** .


## FAQ


### What is AI pull request review?


It is an automated review of a proposed code change, usually delivered as findings on the pull request. Its usefulness depends on repository context, specific review rules and whether the findings identify problems engineers need to fix.


### Can I use AI to review a GitHub pull request?


Yes. Connect a review app such as cubic to the repository, evaluate GitHub's Copilot code review, or maintain your own review workflow. With cubic connected, open a new PR or comment` @cubic-dev-ai review this PR` on an existing one.


### How much does AI pull request review cost?


Billing can depend on seats, credits, reviewed lines or model usage. Estimate the cost using your PR volume and change sizes, including reruns. Check[cubic's current pricing](https://www.cubic.dev/pricing-plans) for its free allowance, paid plans and usage limits.


### Does AI review replace tests or security scanning?


No. Tests check specified behavior, static tools enforce defined checks, and AI review can investigate contextual problems. Keep those checks together and have a person evaluate findings and important changes.


### Can AI review code written by another AI?


Yes, but the review still needs independent verification. Check the failure the reviewer describes, inspect any generated fix, and run tests. Using an AI author and an AI reviewer does not establish that the change is correct.
